# Pistonless steam pump (Savery) (`savery_steam_pump`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: needs safety_valve_boiler; helped by atmospheric_pressure, piston_pump
- Core idea: The simplest way to raise water by fire, with no piston and no moving parts but valves. Fill a closed vessel with steam, shut the steam cock and pour cold water over the vessel: the steam condenses, and air pressure pushes water up a suction pipe through a one-way valve into the vessel (at most 6 to 7 m in practice). Then admit steam again; its pressure drives the water out through a second valve and up the delivery pipe. Every 10 m of delivery height needs one atmosphere of steam pressure. That is its weakness: it must sit deep in the mine within suction height of the water, it needs strong steam that the soldered copper vessels of 1700 could not hold, and it heats and cools the whole vessel at every stroke.
- Pitfalls:
  - Expecting it to drain a deep mine; it suits lifts of 10 to 15 m (fountains, water supply)
  - Soldered joints and no safety valve; Savery's own engines blew their seams
  - Confusing it with Newcomen's engine, which uses a piston and only atmospheric pressure
- History: europe: 1601 – della Porta and 1615 de Caus show steam driving water out of a vessel; 1606 Jerónimo de Ayanz receives a Spanish privilege for steam-driven mine drainage; 1663 Marquis of Worcester's 'water-commanding engine'; 1698 Thomas Savery's patent, described in The Miner's Friend (1702); 1870s the pulsometer revives the principle
- Read:
  - Thomas Savery, The Miner's Friend; or, An Engine to Raise Water by Fire (1702)
  - H. W. Dickinson, A Short History of the Steam Engine (1939)
